article.headline: The Hidden Bear Market Beneath the Dot-Com Boom
article.lede: In the spring of 1998, the S&P 500 was climbing toward new records and the NASDAQ was accelerating into one of history's most spectacular bull runs. Yet one measure most investors ignored — the NYSE *advance-decline line* — had already peaked and begun a two-year decline. Walter Deemer, a founding member of what is now the CMT Association and a 52-year veteran of institutional technical analysis, posted this historical chart in May 2026 with no commentary: the timing speaks for itself.
article.body:
The *advance-decline line* is a *breadth indicator* built on a deceptively simple daily count: the number of NYSE-listed stocks that closed higher minus the number that closed lower, accumulated into a running cumulative total. Each stock counts identically — one advancing issue or one declining issue — regardless of market capitalization. A small regional bank and **Microsoft** (MSFT) contribute the same weight. Cap-weighted indexes like the S&P 500, by contrast, are dominated by their largest constituents; a single mega-cap stock can lift the headline number while hundreds of smaller names quietly deteriorate. The A/D line exists precisely to expose that gap.

The gap that opened in April 1998 was extraordinary. The NYSE cumulative A/D line peaked around April 3, 1998 — approximately 23 months before the NASDAQ reached its all-time high of 5,048.62 on March 10, 2000. As the S&P 500 rose steadily to new records and the NASDAQ surged 85.6% in 1999 alone, the A/D line ground steadily lower. What the headline indexes registered as a roaring bull market was, for the median NYSE-listed stock, already a bear market — declining since spring 1998.

The mechanism was extreme concentration. **Qualcomm** (QCOM) rose 2,619% in 1999; a dozen other large-cap technology and internet names each rose more than 1,000% the same year. By mid-2000, the information technology sector represented 33% of S&P 500 market capitalization against roughly half that share of actual S&P earnings. The top 15 performers accounted for an estimated 70% of the index's entire annual gain in 1999. Wikipedia's entry on the dot-com bubble states the structural paradox plainly: “More stocks fell in value than rose in value as investors sold stocks in slower-growing companies to invest in Internet stocks.” The A/D line counted every one of those losers.

The divergence resolved in the only way it could. The S&P 500 fell approximately 46% from its March 2000 peak to its October 2002 trough; the NASDAQ collapsed 78%. In retrospect the A/D line's warning had been legible, and consistently negative, for nearly two years before the crash — one of the longest breadth divergences in market history. Deemer posted this chart in May 2026, weeks after Bloomberg reported that current S&P 500 breadth had narrowed to its slimmest margin since the dot-com era, and as **Goldman Sachs** (GS) issued a comparable public caution. He offered no caption. The chart supplies its own.

concepts.definition: Each trading day, the number of NYSE-listed stocks that closed higher (advancing issues) minus those that closed lower (declining issues) is calculated as net advances. Those daily figures are then added together into a running cumulative total — the A/D line — which rises when breadth is healthy and falls when more stocks are declining than advancing, regardless of what cap-weighted indexes show.

A divergence occurs when a price index makes new highs but its advance-decline line fails to confirm — meaning fewer stocks are participating in the rally. Technicians treat a sustained bearish divergence as a warning: a narrow rally supported by only a handful of large-cap names tends to be fragile and has historically preceded significant market corrections.

A measurement that tracks how widely a market move is shared across all securities in an index, rather than being driven by the performance of a few large constituents. Breadth indicators are designed to reveal whether a rally or decline has broad participation or is concentrated in a small number of names.

A stock market index in which each component's influence is proportional to its total market capitalization — the share price multiplied by shares outstanding. A company worth $3 trillion affects the index far more than one worth $300 million. This structure means a cap-weighted index can rise while the majority of its component stocks are declining, if the largest names outperform strongly enough.

ticker_msft.name: Microsoft Corporation
ticker_msft.description: Microsoft is a global software, cloud, and AI platform company. Its principal segments are Productivity and Business Processes (Office, LinkedIn, Dynamics), Intelligent Cloud (Azure, server products), and More Personal Computing (Windows, Xbox, Surface). The company is in a structural transition from a capital-light software licensor to a capital-intensive hyperscale cloud and AI infrastructure provider.
ticker_msft.blurb: Microsoft is a global software, cloud, and AI platform company. Its principal segments are Productivity and Business Processes (Office, LinkedIn, Dynamics), Intelligent Cloud (Azure, server products), and More Personal Computing (Windows, Xbox, Surface). The company is in a structural transition from a capital-light software licensor to a capital-intensive hyperscale cloud and AI infrastructure provider.
ticker_msft.recent: As of early May 2026, MSFT trades near $413 — down approximately 25.6% from its July 31, 2025 all-time high of $555.45 and -15.7% YTD — after touching a March 28 correction low of $356.07. The drawdown carried the stock briefly below its 200-week moving average for the first time in roughly 13 years (prior touches: 2009, 2018, 2020, 2022). Revenue grew 18% YoY with Azure +40%, while annualized AI revenue reached approximately $37 billion; calendar-2026 capex is projected near $190 billion and free cash flow contracted -22% YoY. Forward P/E is approximately 24.4.

ticker_qcom.name: QUALCOMM Incorporated
ticker_qcom.blurb: QUALCOMM is the dominant designer of smartphone application processors (Snapdragon) and the world leader in mobile baseband modems — the chips that connect phones to cellular networks. The company operates a dual business model: QCT (chip sales) and QTL (technology licensing), with the latter generating high-margin royalties on every 3G/4G/5G handset sold globally. QUALCOMM is actively diversifying into automotive silicon and edge AI processors to reduce dependence on the handset market, particularly following Apple's decision to develop its own modems.
ticker_qcom.recent: Q2 FY2026 revenue reached $10.6 billion with non-GAAP EPS of $2.65. Automotive revenue hit $1.3 billion (+38% YoY), crossing $5 billion annualised for the first time. The expected partial loss of Apple modem business is weighing on forward EPS consensus, producing near-flat EPS growth estimates (-0.3%) for next fiscal year despite strong automotive and IoT momentum. Forward P/E sits at ~15.7x — undemanding for a franchise with durable licensing revenue.

poster_walterdeemer.blurb: Walter Deemer is a veteran market technician and author of the Deemer Market Timing Model. He posts about technical analysis, market breadth, volume patterns, and historical market comparisons. His account has a modest but engaged following among finance professionals.
poster_walterdeemer.credibility_note: Deemer is a respected figure in technical analysis with decades of experience, but his posts reflect a specific methodological bias toward market timing and breadth indicators.
